When I watch an automated verification pipeline fail, I want to inspect a real regression, not a severed network socket. For a long time, standard test suites suffered from a subtle failure path: tying validation lifetime directly to the terminal session that triggered it. Whenever an interactive caller dropped, the validation run vanished with it. That left the builder with corrupted evidence, forcing operators to treat every disconnected terminal as if it were a defect in the product itself.

That ambiguity destroys trust in test results. If an agent loses its connection mid-flight, we cannot tell whether our code broke or the client simply disappeared. We needed validation that persists regardless of who stays attached to the console.

To fix this, we shipped a standard protocol documented in docs/TESTING.md that decouples the suite lifecycle from caller sessions. Instead of relying on client-bound processes, our backend test runner, test-genie, takes full control of the execution state. Under this design, validation becomes server-owned rather than client-dependent. An operator or agent does not have to maintain an open socket just to keep work alive; they can simply trigger the workload and wait on the durable execution record.

This change anchors validation in verified telemetry rather than brittle connections, ensuring that interrupted sessions no longer distort our operational evidence.

When I kick off a test suite today, I execute vrooli scenario test, which starts a scenario suite and returns once the run is registered. Instead of holding an active terminal hostage while steps execute, the CLI immediately yields back control to the caller. At that exact moment, our execution runner, test-genie, assumes complete authority over the workload.

This handoff is where the architectural shift happens. Because test-genie owns a scenario test run after the command returns, the lifecycle of the suite is no longer tethered to whatever machine invoked it. An automated agent or human builder can trigger the process, record the assigned run identifier, and immediately disconnect without interrupting ongoing execution.

Making test execution server-owned solves a classic failure path in automated workflows. Previously, if an agent session timed out, crashed, or rotated during a long-running suite, the entire run perished with the caller. Now, the suite keeps running in the background, logging every transition and preserving its state inside the platform. The work does not stop simply because the interactive session concluded.

By separating the initiation step from the monitoring step, we treat test runs as durable platform entities rather than ephemeral client side-effects. An operator who triggers a suite can step away, pass the execution context to another process, or wait for the outcome when convenient. The evidence remains addressable on the server throughout its full lifespan, insulating our validation runs from flaky networks and transient client boundaries.

Once an operator records the run identifier, keeping track of execution does not require brittle client-side polling loops. Instead of repeatedly querying an endpoint to see if work finished, we rely on a single blocking synchronization step. Running test-genie runs wait --json blocks once on a server-owned run; the documented alternative to polling. This lets an operator or automated workflow wait efficiently for execution to wrap up, receiving structured output without hammering the platform with repetitive status checks.

This blocking mechanism cleanly separates local caller states from remote workload lifecycles. A cancelled client is not the same thing as an aborted run. If a network blip severs your shell, or if an automated agent shuts down while waiting, the underlying suite does not crash or mark itself as broken. Because the process is server-owned, test-genie keeps driving the validation steps forward. Dropping the connection merely disconnects the listener; it leaves the actual run intact and operating as intended.

When an operator intentionally needs to kill an active suite, they must do so through a direct platform command rather than by terminating their local terminal window. Executing vrooli scenario test abort ends the run itself, as opposed to cancelling the client. This sends an explicit signal to test-genie to stop the scenario, tear down resources, and document that the workload was deliberately terminated.

By distinguishing between client disconnections and explicit stops, we protect the validity of our operational history. An interrupted shell is treated as an infrastructure event, while a stopped run is recorded as an intentional user action. This clarity gives builders confidence that our test logs reflect genuine validation outcomes rather than the health of a local socket connection.

This brings us to the core benefit for automated workflows: reliable handoffs between autonomous agents. When long validation suites generate continuous telemetry, decoupling that execution from any single terminal transforms waiting into a governed platform capability.

In our continuous verification loop, an initiating agent can invoke vrooli scenario test and immediately record the identifier before exiting. A second, downstream agent running in a fresh environment can later invoke test-genie runs wait --json to wait on that exact server-owned run. Because test-genie manages the workload remotely, the second agent receives the complete, uncorrupted log record the moment validation concludes.

This shared record prevents false triage loops. Instead of diagnosing a phantom failure caused by an agent rotation or client reset, the downstream agent inspects the definitive run artifact. It can verify whether the workload completed cleanly or if another operator sent vrooli scenario test abort to halt execution. Every status transition remains attached to the server-owned record rather than vanishing with an ephemeral runner.

By formalizing this flow in docs/TESTING.md, we ensure that our control plane improves validation reliability without demanding persistent terminal attachments. An agent can start a run, hand off responsibility, and allow a peer to evaluate the final evidence. We shipped this approach so builders never have to guess whether a broken suite stems from a real regression or a lost connection. Durable runs preserve the full context, giving every automated actor the exact evidence needed to make grounded operational decisions.
baseline_text:
When you trigger a complex test suite and your terminal connection drops, what happens to the validation you just started? If your testing harness couples the lifecycle of the execution to the active client connection, that validation vanishes into thin air. We built our execution model around the premise that durable validation is a product capability, ensuring that long-running tests persist, stay addressable, and finish cleanly regardless of what happens to the caller.

In this post, I want to walk through how we approach long-running validation in Vrooli, why server-owned runs matter for day-to-day engineering, and how our architecture decouples test orchestration from transient client sessions. The protocol this article summarises is recorded in our central documentation at docs/TESTING.md, and it reflects our conviction that reliable validation requires reliable state.

To understand the shift we made, consider what validation looks like when a test run is tied strictly to an open client session. An engineer or automated agent triggers a suite, the process attaches to the local terminal, and the client waits. If the session terminates, the process dies with it. This coupling introduces real friction: the suite takes longer than an agent session, work is interrupted, logs disappear, and operators are left guessing whether a failure was caused by a genuine software defect or a severed connection.

To solve this, we rely on test-genie, our internal backend service responsible for managing, executing, and tracking test runs. When we invoke the command vrooli scenario test to kick off validation, vrooli scenario test starts a scenario suite and returns once the run is registered. Crucially, test-genie owns a scenario test run after the command returns.

Because test-genie owns a scenario test run after the command returns, the test run maintains its own identity, its own logs, and its own execution lifecycle on the server. The client that initiated the run can safely exit without affecting the validation itself. The run does not disappear with the caller; instead, it continues uninterrupted within test-genie.

This architecture establishes a clean, governed workflow for operators. The workflow is simple: operators start the suite, record its run identifier, and wait once on the server-owned run. When an operator or automation system wants to collect the final outcome, they use test-genie runs wait --json, which blocks once on a server-owned run and serves as the documented alternative to polling.

By using test-genie runs wait --json, an operator does not need to constantly query or poll the system to see if the run has completed. They simply invoke test-genie runs wait --json to block once on the server-owned run until execution finishes. The client receives the complete result in a structured format as soon as test-genie finishes processing the suite.

One of the most important operational distinctions in this design is how we handle cancellations and interruptions. In our system, a cancelled client is not the same thing as an aborted run. If an operator closes their terminal, disconnects an agent, or interrupts the client process that was waiting on a run, only the local client connection is cancelled. The scenario test run itself remains active and intact within test-genie.

If an operator genuinely intends to terminate the execution on the server, they must explicitly issue the abort command. Specifically, vrooli scenario test abort ends the run itself, as opposed to cancelling the client. This explicit separation ensures that an accidental client disconnection never inadvertently destroys an active test run.

This distinction is operational, not cosmetic. A system that treats every disconnected terminal as a failed test loses the difference between infrastructure interruption and a product defect. When a transient network hiccup kills an interactive session, treating that event as a test failure pollutes test metrics and wastes engineering time chasing phantom bugs. Server-owned runs preserve that distinction so the next operator can inspect the evidence and make a grounded decision.

Because the run identifier persists and the state lives inside test-genie, durable evidence for long-running validation is preserved automatically. When a suite takes longer than an agent session, the initial agent can record the run identifier and conclude its session. A later agent or human operator can then pick up that exact run identifier, query test-genie, and resume observation or inspect the completed results. This makes a later handoff possible across different operators, systems, or automated workflows.

Having an addressable, server-owned run fundamentally transforms how we think about test infrastructure. Instead of viewing testing as a synchronous script running inside a fragile local process, we treat testing as an asynchronous, stateful workload managed by a dedicated control plane. The result is a control plane that can improve itself without asking every agent to stay attached to a terminal.

When we look at the complete lifecycle defined in docs/TESTING.md, the benefits compound across our entire development workflow. When an operator runs vrooli scenario test, they get an immediate confirmation and a run identifier. The run is registered, test-genie takes ownership, and the operator is free to disconnect. When it is time to check the outcome, test-genie runs wait --json provides the necessary blocking call to retrieve the output once. And if a run must truly be stopped before completion, vrooli scenario test abort provides the explicit mechanism to end the run itself.

Durable runs turn waiting into a governed capability: the work continues, the evidence remains addressable, and the final decision can be made from the same record that produced it. By ensuring that test-genie owns the execution lifecycle and separating client cancellation from run abortion, we have built a resilient foundation for long-running validation that keeps our engineering decisions grounded in durable, reliable facts.
